extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction-writers, and students/critics of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the craft and method of writing novels: how to choose and manage scene vs panorama, point of view, character and setting treatment, and the placement and economy of incidents. Draws examples and explanations from Flaubert (Madame Bovary) and Thackeray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene holds the place of honour: it is the readiest means of starting an interest and raising a question, and it recurs as the natural vehicle for climaxes and resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the ball, the comices, the theatre evening, Emma’s interview with Léon, the priest/apothecary session in Madame Bovary—each scene articulates the book and furthers the scheme of structure. Use scenes to start interest and to complete what they began. Anti-pattern: treating scenes as merely decorative or isolated moments without structural function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene preparation and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Place an occasion at the point where everything is ready for it so that it will 'thoroughly illuminate a new face of the subject and advance the action by a definite stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scene that is not really wanted or that does nothing in particular weakens a story; lack of prior preparation causes a scene to fail to make its effect. The author should ensure the action is ripe and the scene resonant when introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic versus panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to present episodes as immediate, dramatic scenes (scenic) or as broad, survey-like overviews (panoramic); the novel’s subject often dictates the balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thackeray (Vanity Fair, Pendennis) exemplifies the panoramic, retrospective survey; Dickens tends toward the theatre-like scenic mode. Choose panorama when the aim is a general impression of a society or landscape; choose scene for concentrated, event-driven moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation of scene and summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect and manage alternation between detailed scenes and more rapid chronicle/summary; summaries often prepare or bridge to the next scene or climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scene commonly yields to a chronicle or summary which in turn prepares the way and leads into the occasion that fulfils it. Use summary to carry the book forward while keeping pauses for immediate sight of character daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method and plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist must have a governing principle for mixing methods and should be consistent on some plan, allowing no more latitude than required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer may deliberately confine himself to one method for a theme, but generally liberty to use multiple methods should still be guided by an adopted principle. Critics look for the principle on which methods are mingled and varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and sustain a centre of vision (point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine with which character (if any) the writer will primarily identify; the centre of vision should 'command the subject' and be used consistently unless there is a reason to shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the right centre is obvious (e.g., Emma in Madame Bovary). If the subject can be rendered through one figure’s perspective, there is no need to range further. Haphazard or unnecessary plunges into other characters' minds confuse the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and disguise shifts into interior consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sudden, gratuitous plunges into inner life; when you must shift into a character’s mind, make the transition smooth and not attention-drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary or abrupt changes of focus (throwing off one character and adopting another viewpoint) are disconcerting. Flaubert handles this by keeping the character always at a certain distance even when entering her mind—maintain a subtle transition so the reader is not wrenched out of the shared experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain authorial distance and use irony as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a character’s mind is limited or untrustworthy, keep an authorial aloofness (often via irony) so readers do not become fully identified with that limited consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert makes Emma subjective but with an air of aloofness and a hint of irony to prevent total immersion. The author's valuation should usually be implied in tone rather than asserted in words. Irony lets the author supersede a character's limited vision without awkward dislocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render setting and secondary persons as integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat scenery, town, and supporting characters with as much intensity and specificity as the protagonist—setting can be as central to the subject as the principal figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Madame Bovary the provincial town (Yonville) and its odd types are given sharp definition and belong integrally to the book; they are not mere background or accessories to the heroine. Make environment 'tell beside' the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject determine whether the work is pictorial or dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the irreducible idea of the book is best expressed as a portrait/picture (pictorial) or as an interaction/conflict (dramatic); that choice governs method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is 'the portrait of a woman' the rest of the material should serve to reveal her; if the subject is the conflict between a person and environment, both must be developed as coequal forces. Misidentifying the subject leads to mismatched method and weaker work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of incident: events should serve the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Events and particular incidents should be used to illustrate the subject, not treated as ends in themselves; many incidents may be interchangeable if their role is merely illustrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert’s handling shows that episodes (Rodolphe, Léon, rides to Rouen) are ways of telling the subject, not indispensable pivots. Over-reliance on incident as if each were intrinsically decisive is an anti-pattern; focus on what incidents reveal about the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering and fusion of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods (dramatic, pictorial, panoramic, scenic, authorial comment, interiority) can and often should be blended—laid upon one another—to create stratified effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One watches how methods are alternated, united, imposed one on another; in well-fashioned work method tends to be 'laid upon method' to form layers. The blending should be purposeful and controlled by the subject’s needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare other characters' perspectives for later payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: When a later scene depends on another character’s reaction or viewpoint, establish that character’s inner life or preparatory episodes earlier in the book so the climax lands credibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Charles’s early history and inner mind are narrated so that when he discovers Emma’s letters the final irony and emotional effect are powerful. Early framing of peripheral minds readies them for later narrative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know characters thoroughly when interior rendering is required
rubrics_metrics.description: If you intend to render a character’s interior life, make sure you know them intimately—track the movement of their mind and how they construct fantasies or illusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert’s first care is to make Emma’s mind and imagination visible—how she creates romances, how she feeds on them and how they fail. Interior rendering must be thorough to be convincing; otherwise the author must supplement it from outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt authorial intrusion unless stylistically warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not abruptly abandon the character’s projected perspective to adopt an overt, self-assertive narrator stance unless that licence is integral to the work’s purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open authorial intrusions that 'boast' of freedom (Thackeray sometimes does this deliberately) can damage the reader’s immersion if done carelessly. If you must comment from outside, soften the transition and keep standards consistent so the shift does not feel like an 'ill turn' to the story.
